gap: No result ChatGPT got states any instrument-measured brightness or colour figure for a laptop screen extender; the two lab readings I could open, on earlier models from two of our partner brands, were 152 nits (Parkablogs, Mobile Pixels Duex Plus) and 193.1 cd/m² peak (Notebookcheck, FOPO 12-inch triple), against the 250–300 nits that today's FOPO S1/S7 and Mobile Pixels Duex Max DS are rated at.
standout_why: I opened both cited rival pages, itechguides.com '15 Best Laptop Screen Extenders for 2026' and rottenwifi.com '15 Best Laptop Screen Extenders for 2026'. Every figure on both is a maker or Amazon-listing claim: 300 nits for the Duex Max DS, 350 nits for the Duex Float 2 Pro, and 72% NTSC for the KEFEYA. Neither cites Notebookcheck, Tom's Hardware, PCMag, RTINGS or any colorimeter reading. rottenwifi even tells readers to 'distinguish manufacturer specifications from independent measurements' and then gives none. The Mighty Gadget Duex Float 2 Pro review (2026-08-16) and Notebookcheck's Uperfect M140G12 article (2026-03-01) also repeat only maker specs. A measured figure from a named reviewer is therefore new against every page ChatGPT read.
decides: It doesn't choose between the candidates. The two measurements I could source are of predecessor models (Duex Plus, 2022; FOPO 12-inch triple, 2022), not of anything sold today under $300. What it supports is one caution in the after-section: rated brightness on these attachable panels has not held up when a named reviewer measured it, so a shopper who works near a window should treat 250 versus 300 nits as a weak reason to pick one screen over another. The pick should rest on the video path and on how many displays the laptop can drive.

findings.label: Measured contrast, sRGB coverage and colour error
findings.value: 247:1 contrast (black 0.75 cd/m²); 79% sRGB; ColorChecker ΔE 4.59 (0.84 after calibration); greyscale ΔE 6.8; no PWM
findings.source_title: FOPO 12-inch triple monitor extender review: Clunky and more fragile than standalone portable monitors (Notebookcheck, Allen Ngo, 2022-07-23)
findings.note: X-Rite i1Pro 2 with Calman. Notebookcheck says the best case is a laptop with two USB-C ports that carry DisplayPort, one USB-C cable per screen, and that Windows sees the screens as ordinary external monitors. The 247:1 contrast compares with the 1000:1 that FOPO rates today's S1 and S7 at (our records). This is a different, older panel.

unsourced: Duex Max DS measured sRGB: search results credit Amateur Photographer with a Datacolor Spyder X2 reading of 64% sRGB on the Duex Max (the original, possibly not the DS). Both amateurphotographer.com URLs returned HTTP 403, so the figure isn't usable. Root-Nation's Duex Max DS review also returned 403.
Duex Max DS measured brightness: I found no Notebookcheck, Tom's Hardware, PCMag or RTINGS test. Every page I opened repeats Mobile Pixels' 300-nit rating.

Arzopa A1 15.6-inch measured brightness: a search snippet credits PCMag with 351 nits on a Klein K10-A colorimeter, but pcmag.com and uk.pcmag.com both refuse fetches. The Tom's Hardware A1 review URL returned only its title (148 characters), so its lab figures couldn't be read.

RTINGS Mobile Pixels DUEX Plus review: rtings.com/monitor/reviews/mobile-pixels/duex-plus loaded without its results body, so I have no RTINGS brightness, contrast or ΔE. It covers the original Duex Plus in any case, not the DS.
FOPO S1, S7, S9G: I looked for Notebookcheck, Tom's Hardware, PCMag and colorimeter reviews and found none. The only FOPO lab test is the 2022 12-inch triple above.

UPERFECT 14-inch 2K single extender and AOKER S2: I looked for colorimeter or lab reviews and found only retailer listings and roundups that repeat maker specs (they give 300 to 400 nits and 100% sRGB for the UPERFECT 2K).

Mobile Pixels Trio 3 Pro: Macworld's review appeared in search with 300 nits and 100% sRGB, which are Mobile Pixels specs, and I didn't open it. I found no instrument-measured figures. It is also over $300 ({price:mobile-pixels-trio-3-pro}).
